title: September 11 attacks
summary: Al-Qaeda hijackers flew airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, killing 2,977 people in the deadliest terrorist attack in history.
description: On the morning of 11 September 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers seized four airliners in the United States. Two struck the Twin Towers of New York's World Trade Center, which collapsed within two hours, a third hit the Pentagon outside Washington, D.C., and the fourth crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back. The 2,977 victims came from more than 90 countries. The attacks launched the US-led 'war on terror', including the invasion of Afghanistan within a month, transformed aviation security and intelligence work worldwide, and formed part of the case for the 2003 Iraq War.

title: 9/11 'truther' claims of an inside job
summary: The 9/11 Truth movement claims the US government planned or allowed the attacks and that the towers and 7 World Trade Center were brought down by explosives.
description: Conspiracy theories about the attacks spread online within months and reached a mass audience through films such as 'Loose Change' (2005), giving rise to the self-described 9/11 Truth movement. Its central claims are that the Twin Towers and the 47-storey 7 World Trade Center, which was not hit by a plane, fell too quickly and too symmetrically to have been brought down by fire, implying planted explosives or thermite, and that the US government either carried out the attacks or deliberately let them happen as a pretext for war. Polls in the years after the attacks found that versions of these ideas had a sizeable minority following in the United States and abroad. The claim is placed here at the site of 7 World Trade Center, the building most cited by proponents.
mainstreamView: Investigations by the 9/11 Commission and the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), along with independent peer-reviewed structural engineering studies, found that the jet impacts severed columns and stripped fireproofing from the towers, and the ensuing fires weakened the steel until the upper floors fell onto structures that could not arrest them. NIST attributed the 2001 collapse of 7 World Trade Center to uncontrolled office fires that caused thermal expansion and the failure of a key column. No recorded blast sounds or seismic signals consistent with demolition charges, no cut-charge residues and no other physical evidence of demolition were found, and al-Qaeda's planning of the attacks is documented in detail, including by its own leaders, who claimed responsibility.

title: War in Afghanistan and the Taliban's return
summary: A US-led coalition toppled the Taliban for sheltering al-Qaeda; after 20 years of war the Taliban retook Kabul as Western forces withdrew in 2021.
description: The United States and Britain began air strikes on 7 October 2001 after the Taliban refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, and together with Afghan Northern Alliance forces they drove the Taliban from Kabul within weeks. A NATO-led mission then backed a new Afghan government, but a resurgent Taliban insurgency, with havens in Pakistan, kept the war going for two decades; US special forces killed bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, on 2 May 2011. After the 2020 Doha agreement set a date for US withdrawal, the Afghan army collapsed and the Taliban entered Kabul on 15 August 2021, amid chaotic airlift scenes at Kabul airport. The last US troops left on 30 August, ending America's longest war, and the restored Taliban emirate barred girls from secondary school and women from most public life. Direct war deaths in Afghanistan are estimated at roughly 170,000 or more.

title: China joins the World Trade Organization
summary: After 15 years of negotiations China joined the WTO, binding itself to global trade rules and opening the way to its rise as the world's leading exporter.
description: China first applied in 1986 to rejoin the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and its accession to the WTO, approved at the Doha ministerial conference on 10 November 2001, took effect a month later. In return for lasting access to foreign markets it agreed to cut tariffs, open sectors such as banking and telecommunications to foreign firms and protect intellectual property. Foreign investment and exports surged: China became the world's largest exporter of goods in 2009 and overtook Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010, while hundreds of millions of Chinese moved from farms to factories and out of extreme poverty. Economists have linked the rapid growth of Chinese imports to the loss of manufacturing jobs in the United States and elsewhere, the so-called 'China shock', and disputes over subsidies, intellectual property and market access fed the US–China trade war that began in 2018.
wikipedia: China and the World Trade Organization

title: War and mass killing in Darfur
summary: Sudan's government and allied Janjaweed militias crushed a rebellion in Darfur with mass killings of non-Arab civilians, displacing some two million people.
description: Rebel groups drawn largely from Darfur's Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa peoples rose against the Khartoum government in early 2003, accusing it of marginalising the region. The government responded with air strikes and armed Arab Janjaweed militias, which burned villages and killed, raped and expelled civilians on a vast scale. The United Nations estimated about 300,000 deaths from violence, disease and hunger, and more than two million people were displaced. The US government called the campaign genocide in 2004, while a 2005 UN commission of inquiry found war crimes and crimes against humanity but no government policy of genocide; the International Criminal Court later issued arrest warrants for President Omar al-Bashir, adding a genocide charge in 2010. Janjaweed fighters went on to form the core of the Rapid Support Forces, a party to Sudan's 2023 civil war.

title: Iraq War
summary: A US-led coalition invaded Iraq and overthrew Saddam Hussein, followed by years of insurgency and sectarian war that killed hundreds of thousands.
description: The United States, Britain and allies invaded on 20 March 2003, citing Iraq's alleged weapons of mass destruction and links to terrorism, and Baghdad fell on 9 April. No stockpiles of such weapons were found, and the war's justification remains widely criticised. The occupation faced a Sunni insurgency, including al-Qaeda in Iraq, and a sectarian civil war that peaked in 2006–07 before a US troop 'surge' and alliances with Sunni tribes reduced the violence; Saddam Hussein was captured in 2003 and executed in 2006. US forces withdrew in December 2011. Estimates of Iraqi deaths vary widely, from more than 100,000 documented civilian deaths to several hundred thousand in survey-based studies, and the turmoil helped give rise to the Islamic State.

title: Human Genome Project completed
summary: The international Human Genome Project announced an essentially complete sequence of the roughly 3 billion DNA letters of the human genome.
description: Launched in 1990 and led by the US National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy with partners including Britain's Sanger Centre, the project published a working draft in 2001 alongside a rival private effort by Celera Genomics. Its completion was declared in April 2003, fifty years after the discovery of DNA's double-helix structure. The sequence showed that humans have only about 20,000 protein-coding genes and became the foundation of modern genomics, medical genetics and the study of human ancestry. The cost of sequencing a genome has since fallen from billions of dollars to a few hundred, and the remaining gaps were filled by the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium in 2022, with the Y chromosome completed in 2023.

title: Facebook launches: the social-media age
summary: Mark Zuckerberg and fellow Harvard students launched 'TheFacebook', which grew into the largest of the social networks that reshaped communication.
description: Facebook began as a network for Harvard students and opened to anyone aged 13 or over in September 2006. It was part of a wave of 'Web 2.0' platforms built on content created by their users, including YouTube (2005), Twitter (2006), Instagram (2010) and later TikTok, whose international version launched in 2017. By the 2020s billions of people used social media daily, transforming news, advertising, politics, activism and personal life. The platforms have also been criticised for spreading misinformation, harming young people's mental health and enabling mass collection of personal data, as exposed in the Cambridge Analytica scandal of 2018.

title: Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami
summary: A magnitude 9.1–9.3 earthquake off Sumatra sent tsunamis across the Indian Ocean, killing about 230,000 people in 14 countries.
description: The earthquake ruptured some 1,300 km of the Sunda megathrust, where the India Plate dives beneath the Burma microplate, and ranks among the three largest earthquakes recorded by seismographs. Waves up to 30 m high struck Aceh in Indonesia within minutes and reached Sri Lanka, India, Thailand and the coast of East Africa within hours. Indonesia suffered by far the most deaths, followed by Sri Lanka, India and Thailand, where many foreign tourists were among the victims. Because the Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning system, most people had no warning; one coordinated by UNESCO became operational in 2006.

title: Hurricane Katrina floods New Orleans
summary: Hurricane Katrina struck the US Gulf Coast; failed levees flooded about 80% of New Orleans and around 1,400 people died.
description: Katrina made landfall in southeast Louisiana as a Category 3 hurricane on 29 August 2005, after reaching Category 5 strength over the Gulf of Mexico. Its storm surge devastated the Mississippi coast, and breaches in the federally built levees and floodwalls flooded about 80% of New Orleans, stranding tens of thousands of residents, many of them poor and Black. The slow government response became a national scandal. With damage of about US$125 billion, Katrina was one of the costliest natural disasters in US history, and the population of New Orleans took more than a decade to partly recover.

title: Apple unveils the iPhone: the smartphone era
summary: Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone, a touchscreen phone, music player and internet device that set the template for the modern smartphone.
description: Smartphones from BlackBerry, Nokia and others already existed, but the iPhone's multi-touch screen and full web browser, followed in 2008 by the App Store, changed how people used mobile devices. Google's Android, first sold on a phone in 2008, brought the same model to a vast range of cheaper handsets. By the 2020s more than half of humanity used a smartphone, giving billions of people, many in Asia and Africa, their first access to the internet along with mobile payments, maps and social media. Smartphones reshaped industries from photography and music to taxis and retail, and changed daily life and attention in ways still being studied.

title: Sichuan earthquake devastates western China
summary: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck Sichuan, China, killing about 69,000 people and leaving 18,000 missing, among them thousands of children in collapsed schools.
description: The earthquake struck in the afternoon on the Longmenshan Fault, where the Tibetan Plateau pushes against the Sichuan Basin, with its epicentre in Wenchuan County, and it ruptured about 240 km of the fault. Mountain towns such as Beichuan were flattened or buried by landslides, and landslide-dammed 'quake lakes' threatened communities downstream. The official toll was about 69,000 dead, 18,000 missing and 374,000 injured, and millions of people were left homeless. The government acknowledged in 2009 that more than 5,000 students had died or were missing, many in poorly built schools that collapsed while nearby buildings stood, and parents and activists such as the artist Ai Weiwei who pressed for accountability were harassed or detained. China mounted a vast rescue effort and accepted foreign help, three months before Beijing hosted the 2008 Summer Olympics.

title: Global financial crisis
summary: The collapse of the US housing bubble and the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers set off a global banking panic and the deepest recession since the 1930s.
description: Years of lax mortgage lending and complex securities built on subprime loans left banks worldwide exposed when US house prices began to fall in 2006. Strains that started in 2007 turned to panic after Lehman Brothers filed for the largest bankruptcy in US history on 15 September 2008, forcing governments to rescue banks and the insurer AIG and central banks to cut interest rates to near zero. World output shrank in 2009, trade collapsed and unemployment soared in many countries. The aftershocks included the European debt crisis that broke out in 2009–10, in which Greece, Ireland, Portugal and, in 2013, Cyprus needed international bailouts and the survival of the euro was questioned, as well as years of austerity and new bank regulation such as the Dodd–Frank Act and Basel III.

title: Barack Obama elected US president
summary: Barack Obama won the US presidential election, becoming the first African American to be elected president of the United States.
description: Obama, a first-term senator from Illinois, defeated the Republican John McCain amid the financial crisis and widespread opposition to the Iraq War, and gave his victory speech to a vast crowd in Chicago's Grant Park. He took office on 20 January 2009 and served two terms. His administration passed an economic stimulus package and the Affordable Care Act of 2010, which greatly expanded health insurance coverage, and he was awarded the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize. His election was widely seen as a milestone for a country with a history of slavery and segregation.

title: Bitcoin's genesis block is mined
summary: The pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin, the first decentralised cryptocurrency, by mining its first 'genesis' block.
description: Bitcoin was described in a white paper published in October 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, whose real identity remains unknown. It records transactions on a public, distributed ledger, the blockchain, secured by 'proof-of-work' computation rather than by a bank or government; the genesis block embedded a headline from The Times of London about bank bailouts. After early use mainly by enthusiasts and on illicit online markets, Bitcoin and thousands of later cryptocurrencies grew into a speculative market worth trillions of US dollars at its peaks. El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021 but scaled the policy back in 2025, making its acceptance voluntary under an IMF loan deal, while critics point to its price volatility, use in crime and fraud, and the large electricity consumption of mining. As a network running worldwide it has no single location; London marks the newspaper quoted in the first block.

title: Haiti earthquake
summary: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake devastated Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince; estimates of the dead range from under 100,000 to over 300,000.
description: The shallow quake struck about 25 km west of the densely populated capital, where poorly built concrete structures collapsed, including the National Palace, the cathedral and the headquarters of the UN peacekeeping mission. The death toll is highly uncertain: the Haitian government gave a figure of about 316,000, while independent studies estimated between about 46,000 and 160,000. More than a million people were left homeless in the poorest country in the Americas. A large international relief effort followed, but recovery was slow, and a cholera epidemic introduced in late 2010 by UN peacekeepers killed nearly 10,000 more people.

title: MMR–autism claim: Lancet retracts Wakefield paper
summary: The Lancet retracted Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper suggesting a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, but the discredited claim still fuels vaccine fears.
description: In February 1998 the London gastroenterologist Andrew Wakefield and 12 co-authors published a study of 12 children treated at the Royal Free Hospital, and at a press conference Wakefield suggested that the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine might trigger bowel disease and autism and urged parents to choose separate jabs. Heavy media coverage followed, and MMR uptake in England fell to about 80% by 2003–04. Investigations by the journalist Brian Deer from 2004 revealed that Wakefield had been paid by lawyers preparing to sue vaccine makers and that the children's records did not match what was published. In January 2010 Britain's General Medical Council found that he had acted dishonestly and irresponsibly, The Lancet fully retracted the paper on 2 February, and he was struck off the medical register that May. Wakefield moved to the United States, where he continued to promote the claim, including in the 2016 film 'Vaxxed', and it remains central to the anti-vaccine movement. The marker is at the Royal Free Hospital in London, where the study was carried out.
mainstreamView: Large studies covering millions of children have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism, including Danish cohort studies of more than 537,000 children in 2002 and more than 650,000 in 2019, the latter also finding no raised risk among children with autistic siblings, and reviews by Cochrane and the US Institute of Medicine reached the same conclusion. Wakefield's results were never replicated, most of his co-authors withdrew its interpretation in 2004, and the BMJ described the study in 2011 as an 'elaborate fraud'. The first signs of autism often become noticeable around the age at which MMR is given, which explains the coincidental timing, and rising autism diagnoses largely reflect broader diagnostic criteria and greater awareness. Falling vaccination rates have been followed by outbreaks of measles, which can kill or cause brain damage, and the disease was declared endemic again in England and Wales in 2008.

title: Arab Spring
summary: Mass protests across the Arab world toppled rulers in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen and set off civil wars in Libya, Syria and Yemen.
description: The wave began after the street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in Sidi Bouzid, Tunisia, on 17 December 2010; President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali fled on 14 January 2011, and Egypt's Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February after 18 days of protest centred on Cairo's Tahrir Square. Uprisings followed in Libya, where NATO air power helped rebels overthrow Muammar Gaddafi, and in Yemen, Bahrain and Syria. Social media and satellite television helped protesters organise and spread their message across the region. Outcomes varied widely: Tunisia built a democracy that lasted about a decade, Egypt's military retook power in 2013, Bahrain's protests were crushed with Saudi help, and Syria, Libya and Yemen descended into prolonged wars.

title: Tōhoku earthquake, tsunami and Fukushima disaster
summary: Japan's largest recorded earthquake, magnitude 9.0–9.1, unleashed a tsunami that killed about 18,500 people and caused meltdowns at Fukushima Daiichi.
description: The earthquake struck off the Pacific coast of Tōhoku on 11 March 2011, and tsunami waves reaching up to about 40 m swept over towns along Japan's northeast coast. Some 18,500 people died or went missing, most of them drowned. At the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant the tsunami knocked out backup power, leading to meltdowns in three reactors and hydrogen explosions, the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl, and more than 150,000 people were evacuated. Germany brought forward its exit from nuclear power, completed in 2023, and other countries reviewed their programmes, while Japan faced a decades-long clean-up, including a release of treated water into the sea that began in 2023.

title: Syrian civil war
summary: A crackdown on protests escalated into a multi-sided war that killed an estimated half a million people and drove half of Syrians from their homes.
description: Protests against President Bashar al-Assad began in March 2011, and the government's violent response drew the country into war between the regime, a fragmented rebel opposition, Kurdish-led forces and jihadist groups including the Islamic State. Foreign powers intervened on every side: Iran, Hezbollah and, from 2015, Russia backed Assad, while Turkey, Gulf states and the United States supported various opponents. The regime used barrel bombs and chemical weapons, including the 2013 sarin attack on Ghouta, and more than 6 million Syrians became refugees, many in Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Europe. After years of stalemate, a rapid rebel offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham captured Damascus on 8 December 2024 and Assad fled to Russia, ending more than five decades of rule by his family. Death toll estimates range from about 300,000 documented civilian deaths to more than 600,000 in total.

title: CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing
summary: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that the bacterial CRISPR–Cas9 system can be programmed to cut DNA at chosen sites.
description: CRISPR sequences are part of a bacterial immune system against viruses, and in a 2012 paper in Science, Charpentier, Doudna and colleagues showed that the Cas9 enzyme, guided by a designed RNA, could cut a chosen DNA sequence. In early 2013 teams led by Feng Zhang and George Church used it to edit the genomes of human cells, making gene editing far cheaper, faster and more precise than earlier methods. The technique spread rapidly through biology, agriculture and medicine, and the first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassaemia, was approved in 2023. In 2018 the Chinese scientist He Jiankui drew worldwide condemnation for creating the first gene-edited babies. Charpentier and Doudna received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

title: Higgs boson discovered at CERN
summary: Physicists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced the discovery of the Higgs boson, the last missing particle of the Standard Model.
description: The ATLAS and CMS experiments independently observed a new particle with a mass of about 125 GeV, produced in proton collisions in the 27-km Large Hadron Collider beneath the French–Swiss border near Geneva. Its properties matched the boson predicted in 1964 by Peter Higgs, François Englert, Robert Brout and others as a sign of the field that gives elementary particles their mass. Higgs and Englert received the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics. The discovery completed the Standard Model of particle physics, although questions such as the nature of dark matter lie beyond it.

title: 2012 Maya 'end of the world' prophecy
summary: Claims that the Maya calendar foretold the end of the world or a cosmic transformation on 21 December 2012 drew a worldwide following before the date passed.
description: The date marked the end of the 13th bʼakʼtun, a cycle of about 394 years in the Maya Long Count calendar, which on the usual correlation fell on 21 or 23 December 2012. From the 1970s New Age writers such as José Argüelles and Terence McKenna linked it to a coming spiritual awakening, and in the 2000s books, websites, documentaries and the 2009 disaster film '2012' popularised doomsday versions involving a collision with a rogue planet called Nibiru, a rare 'galactic alignment', a sudden reversal of Earth's magnetic poles or giant solar flares. Polls suggested that a noticeable minority of people in many countries feared the world might end, and NASA said it received many anxious questions, some from frightened children. On the day thousands of visitors gathered at Maya sites such as Chichén Itzá, where the marker is placed, while French authorities closed the peak above the village of Bugarach, rumoured to be a refuge from which aliens would rescue the faithful.
mainstreamView: Maya scholars explain that the end of a bʼakʼtun completed a calendar cycle, like an odometer rolling over, rather than marking an end of time, and Classic Maya inscriptions refer to dates far beyond 2012, including one at Palenque that reaches the year 4772 CE. The only known ancient text mentioning the date, Monument 6 at Tortuguero in Mexico, describes the descent of a deity without any prediction of catastrophe, and modern Maya communities did not treat it as a doomsday. Astronomers pointed out that no planet called Nibiru exists, since an object on a collision course would already have been plainly visible; that the Sun's position near the galactic equator at the December solstice changes only slowly over centuries and has no physical effect; and that there was no sign of an imminent magnetic reversal or unusual solar activity. The date passed without incident.

title: Francis becomes the first pope from the Americas
summary: Argentina's Jorge Mario Bergoglio was elected Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas and the first Jesuit pope, after Benedict XVI resigned.
description: Benedict XVI stepped down on 28 February 2013, citing his age, the first pope to resign since Gregory XII in 1415, and the cardinals meeting in the Sistine Chapel chose the archbishop of Buenos Aires on the fifth ballot. Taking his name from Francis of Assisi, he was also the first pope from outside Europe since the 8th century. As leader of some 1.3 billion Catholics he stressed mercy and the poor, defended migrants and called for action on climate change in the 2015 encyclical Laudato si', while pursuing reform of Vatican finances and facing continued anger over clerical sexual abuse and resistance from conservative Catholics. He died on 21 April 2025, Easter Monday, and on 8 May the cardinals elected the Chicago-born Robert Prevost, who took the name Leo XIV and became the first pope from the United States.

title: West African Ebola epidemic
summary: The largest Ebola outbreak in history spread from rural Guinea to Liberia and Sierra Leone, infecting about 28,600 people and killing more than 11,300.
description: The epidemic is thought to have begun with a toddler infected in the village of Meliandou, Guinea, in December 2013, possibly through contact with bats, but it was not identified as Ebola until March 2014. Unlike earlier outbreaks in remote parts of Central Africa, it reached crowded capitals such as Conakry, Monrovia and Freetown, overwhelming weak health systems. The WHO declared an international public health emergency in August 2014, and a large international response with treatment centres, safe burial teams and contact tracing gradually brought the outbreak under control. It also spurred an effective Ebola vaccine, rVSV-ZEBOV, first trialled in Guinea in 2015.

title: Russia seizes and annexes Crimea
summary: Russian troops without insignia seized Crimea from Ukraine, and after a disputed referendum Russia annexed the peninsula in March 2014.
description: After Ukraine's pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych was ousted by the Euromaidan protests in February 2014, unmarked Russian soldiers took control of Crimea's parliament, airports and Ukrainian military bases. A referendum held on 16 March under Russian occupation reported overwhelming support for joining Russia, and Russia formally annexed Crimea and Sevastopol on 18 March. Ukraine and most of the international community, through a UN General Assembly resolution, rejected the annexation as illegal. Within weeks Russian-backed separatists, supported by Russian forces, began a war in Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, the opening phase of the Russo-Ukrainian War. In July 2014 Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 was shot down over Donbas, killing all 298 people aboard.
wikipedia: Annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation

title: Islamic State declares a 'caliphate'
summary: The jihadist Islamic State seized Mosul and much of Iraq and Syria, proclaiming a caliphate that ruled millions until its territorial defeat in 2019.
description: Growing out of al-Qaeda in Iraq and exploiting the Syrian civil war, the group captured Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city, on 10 June 2014, and its leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi proclaimed a caliphate weeks later. It ruled through terror, carrying out mass executions, a genocide against the Yazidis of Sinjar and the enslavement of women, and destroying ancient sites such as Palmyra and Nimrud. It also inspired or directed attacks abroad, including the November 2015 Paris attacks. A US-led coalition, Iraqi forces and Kurdish-led fighters gradually retook its territory, including Mosul and Raqqa in 2017, and its last stronghold, Baghuz in eastern Syria, fell in March 2019. Affiliates and insurgent cells remained active in Iraq, Syria, Africa and Afghanistan.

title: Gravitational waves detected
summary: The twin LIGO detectors in the United States recorded gravitational waves from two merging black holes, confirming a century-old prediction of Einstein.
description: The signal, named GW150914, came from two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging roughly 1.3 billion light-years away, and it stretched and squeezed the LIGO detectors in Louisiana and Washington State by about a thousandth of the width of a proton. It was the first direct detection of gravitational waves, which Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity predicted in 1916, and the first observation of a black-hole merger. Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work. In 2017 LIGO and Europe's Virgo detector also caught colliding neutron stars whose light was seen by telescopes worldwide, opening the era of multi-messenger astronomy.

title: Paris Agreement on climate change
summary: Nearly every nation agreed in Paris to limit global warming to well below 2 °C, aiming for 1.5 °C, through nationally set emission targets.
description: Adopted at the COP21 climate summit by the 196 parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the agreement replaced the Kyoto Protocol's binding targets for rich countries with pledges from all countries, called nationally determined contributions, to be strengthened every five years. It entered into force on 4 November 2016. The United States withdrew during Donald Trump's first term, rejoined under President Joe Biden in 2021, and withdrew again after Trump returned to office in January 2025, with the exit taking effect a year later, in January 2026. Pledges made under the agreement have lowered projected warming, but they remain well short of what the 1.5 °C goal requires.

title: SpaceX lands an orbital rocket booster
summary: A SpaceX Falcon 9 first stage flew back and landed upright at Cape Canaveral after launching satellites, the first landing of an orbital-class booster.
description: Rocket stages had always been discarded after a single flight, and SpaceX, founded by Elon Musk in 2002, set out to cut costs by recovering and reusing them. After the December 2015 landing it achieved landings on ocean drone ships in 2016 and the first reflight of a used orbital booster in 2017, and individual boosters were later flown more than 20 times. Reuse helped SpaceX dominate the global launch market, carry astronauts to the International Space Station from 2020 and deploy thousands of Starlink internet satellites. Blue Origin had landed its smaller, suborbital New Shepard booster a month earlier.

title: Britain votes to leave the European Union
summary: In a referendum, 51.9% of UK voters chose to leave the European Union, leading to Britain's departure on 31 January 2020.
description: Prime Minister David Cameron called the referendum, which turned on questions of sovereignty, immigration and the economy; England and Wales voted to leave, while Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain. Cameron resigned, and years of fraught negotiations followed, notably over avoiding a hard border on the island of Ireland. After Boris Johnson's Conservatives won the December 2019 general election, the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020 and its single market and customs union at the end of that year. Brexit was the first departure of a member state from the EU and reshaped British politics and trade.

title: Donald Trump elected US president
summary: Businessman and television personality Donald Trump defeated Hillary Clinton to win the US presidency on a nationalist 'America First' platform.
description: Trump, who had never held public office, won the Electoral College while losing the national popular vote by about 2.9 million votes, a result that surprised most forecasters. His campaign combined opposition to immigration and free-trade deals with attacks on political and media elites, and it formed part of a wider rise of populist movements that included the Brexit vote earlier that year. As president from 2017 to 2021 he cut taxes, appointed three Supreme Court justices, imposed tariffs on China and withdrew from the Paris Agreement and the Iran nuclear deal. He lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, and his refusal to accept the result culminated in the attack on the US Capitol by his supporters on 6 January 2021.

title: Colombia's peace deal with the FARC
summary: Colombia's government and the FARC guerrillas signed a peace agreement ending more than 50 years of war with Latin America's largest rebel group.
description: Negotiations held in Havana from 2012 produced a deal that voters narrowly rejected in a referendum on 2 October 2016; a revised agreement was signed in Bogotá on 24 November and ratified by Congress. President Juan Manuel Santos received the 2016 Nobel Peace Prize. In 2017 thousands of FARC fighters handed over their weapons under UN supervision, and the group became a political party. The wider conflict between guerrillas, paramilitaries and the state had killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions, and violence by FARC dissidents, other armed groups and drug traffickers continued after the deal.

title: Myanmar's army drives out the Rohingya
summary: After militant attacks, Myanmar's army killed thousands of Rohingya Muslims and burned hundreds of villages, driving more than 700,000 people into Bangladesh.
description: The Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority in Myanmar's Rakhine State, had been largely denied citizenship since a 1982 law and had suffered earlier waves of violence, including in 2012 and 2016. After the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army attacked some 30 police posts on 25 August 2017, the army and local militias launched what they called 'clearance operations', with mass killings, rape and the burning of hundreds of villages; Médecins Sans Frontières estimated that at least 6,700 Rohingya were killed in the first month alone. More than 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh within months, and the camps around Kutupalong near Cox's Bazar became the largest refugee settlement in the world. A UN fact-finding mission concluded in 2018 that the army's commander, Min Aung Hlaing, and other generals should be investigated and prosecuted for genocide, in 2019 the Gambia brought a case against Myanmar under the Genocide Convention at the International Court of Justice, and in 2022 the United States formally called the campaign genocide. Myanmar's government, whose leader Aung San Suu Kyi defended it at the court in 2019, denied genocide, and Min Aung Hlaing went on to seize power in a coup in 2021. The marker is at Maungdaw in northern Rakhine, at the centre of the violence.

title: #MeToo movement goes viral
summary: Reports of sexual abuse by film producer Harvey Weinstein sparked #MeToo, in which millions shared experiences of sexual harassment and assault.
description: After The New York Times and The New Yorker published allegations against Weinstein in October 2017, the actress Alyssa Milano invited women to reply 'me too' on Twitter, adopting a phrase used by the activist Tarana Burke since 2006. The hashtag was used millions of times within days and spread to dozens of countries, with local movements in France, India, China, South Korea and elsewhere. Many powerful men in entertainment, media, politics and business lost their positions, and Weinstein was convicted of rape in Los Angeles in 2022. The movement prompted changes to workplace policies and laws on harassment and non-disclosure agreements, along with debates about due process.

title: QAnon conspiracy theory emerges
summary: Anonymous 'Q' posts on 4chan spawned QAnon, which claims a secret cabal of Satan-worshipping, child-trafficking elites runs the world and opposes Trump.
description: The posts, signed 'Q' and claiming to come from a government insider with top-level 'Q clearance', began on 28 October 2017 and built on the 2016 'Pizzagate' hoax about a Washington pizzeria. Followers believed that Donald Trump was secretly fighting the cabal and that a day of reckoning, 'the Storm', would bring mass arrests and executions of prominent Democrats and celebrities. Spread through social media, the movement grew during the COVID-19 pandemic, gained adherents in Europe and elsewhere, and many believers took part in the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol. An FBI bulletin in 2019 identified conspiracy theories of this kind as a potential domestic terrorism threat.
mainstreamView: None of Q's specific predictions came true: the promised mass arrests, military tribunals and 'Storm' never happened, and dates set for them repeatedly passed without event. Journalists, investigators and courts have found no evidence of an elite child-trafficking cabal of the kind described, and the pizzeria at the centre of 'Pizzagate' did not even have the basement where abuse was alleged to occur. Linguistic analyses published in 2022 attributed the Q posts mainly to people connected with the message boards that hosted them rather than to any government insider, and researchers see QAnon as a revival of old secret-cabal and antisemitic 'blood libel' tropes.

title: Flat Earth revival
summary: Spread by YouTube videos and social media, the belief that Earth is a flat disc rather than a globe gained a vocal online following in the 2010s.
description: Modern flat-Earth ideas descend from the 19th-century English writer Samuel Rowbotham and the flat-Earth society founded in Britain in 1956, but they reached a new audience from about 2014 through online videos. Most adherents picture a disc with the North Pole at its centre and Antarctica as a wall of ice around the edge, and hold that space agencies fake photographs of a spherical Earth. The first Flat Earth International Conference was held in Raleigh, North Carolina, in November 2017, and several celebrities voiced support. The documentary 'Behind the Curve' (2018) followed believers whose own experiments produced results consistent with a rotating, round Earth.
mainstreamView: Earth's roughly spherical shape has been known since ancient Greek times, when Eratosthenes estimated its circumference from the angles of shadows, and it is confirmed by ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon, the curved shadow Earth casts on the Moon during lunar eclipses, different stars being visible from different latitudes, time zones and routine circumnavigation by ship and aircraft. Today it is measured directly by satellite geodesy and GPS and photographed from space by agencies and companies in many rival countries with no reason to collude. Researchers regard the revival as a product of distrust in institutions and online echo chambers rather than of any new evidence.

title: First image of a black hole
summary: The Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole: the shadow of the 6.5-billion-solar-mass giant at the centre of galaxy M87.
description: The Event Horizon Telescope links radio observatories from Hawaii and Arizona to Chile's ALMA array, Spain and the South Pole into a virtual telescope the size of Earth, using very-long-baseline interferometry. Data recorded in April 2017 took two years to process into the image, which shows a bright ring of hot gas around a dark shadow some 55 million light-years away. Its size and shape matched the predictions of Einstein's general relativity. In 2022 the collaboration released a similar image of Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way.

title: Australia's Black Summer bushfires
summary: Australia's Black Summer fires burned roughly 19–24 million hectares, killed 33 people directly and killed or displaced nearly 3 billion animals.
description: After Australia's hottest and driest year on record in 2019, fires burned across New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and other states, peaking around New Year, when thousands of people sheltered on beaches at towns such as Mallacoota. Smoke blanketed Sydney and Canberra for weeks, was linked to hundreds of additional deaths, and drifted as far as South America. Attribution studies concluded that human-caused climate change had made the extreme fire weather at least 30% more likely. Estimates of the burned area vary from about 19 to 24 million hectares depending on what is counted, and the fires pushed several threatened species closer to extinction.

title: Origin of SARS-CoV-2: spillover or lab leak?
summary: Whether the COVID-19 virus jumped to humans from animals sold at a Wuhan market or escaped from a laboratory remains unresolved.
description: SARS-CoV-2 belongs to a family of bat coronaviruses, and its closest known relatives have been found in bats in Yunnan and Laos. Many of the earliest known cases clustered around Wuhan's Huanan market, where live wild animals such as raccoon dogs were sold, but the city is also home to the Wuhan Institute of Virology, which collected and experimented on bat coronaviruses. China restricted independent investigation, and a 2021 WHO–China joint study that called a laboratory incident 'extremely unlikely' was criticised as premature, including by the WHO's director-general. No infected intermediate animal and no laboratory record of the virus before the outbreak have been found, and the question has become politically charged, especially in the United States.
mainstreamView: Most virologists who have published on the question favour natural zoonotic spillover, citing the clustering of early cases around the Huanan market, the presence of two early viral lineages consistent with more than one animal-to-human jump, and market-stall samples that contained both the virus and genetic material from susceptible animals. Proponents of a laboratory-related origin point to the proximity of the Wuhan Institute of Virology, its coronavirus research and the lack of an identified infected animal. US intelligence agencies have been split, some leaning toward a lab-related origin and others toward natural spillover, all with low or moderate confidence, and a 2025 WHO advisory group judged spillover best supported by the available evidence while saying a lab leak could not be ruled out without data China has not shared.

title: COVID-19 pandemic
summary: A new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, emerged in Wuhan, China, and spread worldwide, causing the deadliest respiratory pandemic since the 1918 influenza.
description: Cases of an unusual pneumonia in Wuhan were reported in December 2019, and the WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020 as the virus spread to every continent. Governments imposed lockdowns, border closures and school closures affecting billions of people, and the world economy suffered its deepest recession since the Second World War. About 7 million deaths were officially reported, but excess-mortality studies suggest the true toll was far higher, with the WHO estimating about 15 million excess deaths in 2020–21 alone. Vaccines, first given under emergency or early approvals in China and Russia from mid-2020 and rolled out widely from December 2020, and growing immunity reduced deaths, and the WHO ended the global health emergency on 5 May 2023, although the virus continues to circulate.

title: 5G–COVID conspiracy theories and mast arson
summary: Conspiracy theorists claimed 5G mobile networks caused or spread COVID-19, leading to arson attacks on phone masts, especially in Britain.
description: Claims that radio waves from new 5G networks were harmful predated the pandemic, and in early 2020 they merged with COVID-19: posts noted that Wuhan had recently rolled out 5G and suggested that the radiation weakened immune systems or spread the virus itself, or that the pandemic was a cover for installing the networks. Amplified by celebrities and social media, the claims led to dozens of arson attacks on mobile phone masts in the United Kingdom in April 2020, starting in Birmingham and Merseyside, as well as attacks in the Netherlands and elsewhere and the harassment of telecom engineers. They formed part of a wider wave of pandemic misinformation that included claims that the virus was a hoax and that vaccines contained microchips.
mainstreamView: COVID-19 is caused by a virus, SARS-CoV-2, which spreads between people through respiratory droplets and aerosols; radio waves cannot carry or create a virus. The disease spread widely in places with little or no 5G coverage, such as Iran, and 5G uses non-ionising radio frequencies at power levels within international exposure limits, which do not damage cells or suppress the immune system. The WHO, national health agencies and telecom regulators rejected the claims, and many of the masts that were burned did not carry 5G equipment at all.

title: AlphaFold transforms protein structure prediction
summary: DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted protein structures from their amino-acid sequences with near-experimental accuracy, largely solving a 50-year-old problem.
description: At the CASP14 assessment in late 2020, AlphaFold 2 far outperformed every other method at predicting how chains of amino acids fold into the three-dimensional shapes that determine how proteins work, a challenge biologists had pursued for about 50 years. DeepMind and the European Bioinformatics Institute then released free predicted structures, growing by 2022 to more than 200 million proteins, nearly every one known to science. The tool accelerated research in drug discovery, enzyme design and basic biology and became one of the most prominent examples of artificial intelligence applied to science. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with the protein designer David Baker.

title: mRNA vaccines against COVID-19
summary: In Coventry, Margaret Keenan became the first person to receive the newly approved Pfizer–BioNTech mRNA vaccine outside a clinical trial.
description: The Pfizer–BioNTech and Moderna vaccines deliver messenger RNA, wrapped in lipid nanoparticles, that instructs cells to make the coronavirus spike protein and so trains the immune system; the approach built on decades of research, including Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman's discovery that modified nucleosides stop injected mRNA from triggering harmful inflammation. Both vaccines showed about 95% efficacy against symptomatic disease in large trials, and on 8 December 2020, after Britain became the first country to approve it, the 90-year-old Keenan became the first person to receive the Pfizer–BioNTech vaccine outside a trial; China and Russia had already begun giving their own vaccines under emergency or early approvals from the summer of 2020. More than 13 billion doses of COVID-19 vaccines of all types were given worldwide by 2023, although access in poorer countries lagged badly. One modelling study estimated that vaccines prevented around 14–20 million deaths in their first year. Karikó and Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

title: James Webb Space Telescope launched
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope, the largest ever launched, lifted off from French Guiana to study the first galaxies and distant planets in infrared light.
description: Built by NASA with the European and Canadian space agencies, the telescope has a 6.5-metre segmented, gold-coated mirror and a sunshield the size of a tennis court, which unfolded in a complex sequence after launch on an Ariane 5 rocket. It orbits near the Sun–Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million km from Earth, where it is kept extremely cold to detect faint infrared light. Its first images were released in July 2022, followed by discoveries of unexpectedly bright galaxies within about 300 million years of the Big Bang and detailed measurements of exoplanet atmospheres. Begun in the 1990s, the project ran years late and cost about US$10 billion.

title: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai eruption
summary: An undersea volcano in Tonga exploded with a force that sent a pressure wave around the world and a plume into the mesosphere.
description: The eruption blasted ash and water vapour to a record height of about 57 km and generated an atmospheric pressure wave that circled the globe several times and was recorded by barometers worldwide. It triggered tsunamis across the Pacific, devastating parts of Tonga, causing deaths as far away as Peru and cutting Tonga's undersea internet cable. Its atmospheric explosion was the largest recorded by modern instruments, comparable to that of Krakatoa in 1883, although Pinatubo in 1991 erupted more material. It also injected some 146 million tonnes of water vapour into the stratosphere, raising its water content by about 10%.
wikipedia: 2022 Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai eruption and tsunami

title: Russia launches full-scale invasion of Ukraine
summary: Russia invaded Ukraine on a massive scale, starting the largest war in Europe since 1945, with hundreds of thousands of casualties.
description: Escalating the conflict it began in 2014, Russia attacked from Belarus, Russia and Crimea, but Ukrainian forces halted the advance on Kyiv and drove Russian troops from the north by April 2022, then recaptured territory around Kharkiv and Kherson that autumn. Russia declared the annexation of four partly occupied Ukrainian regions in September 2022, and the front settled into grinding warfare dominated by artillery, trenches and drones. More than six million Ukrainians became refugees abroad, and Western states imposed sweeping sanctions on Russia while supplying Ukraine with weapons and aid. The war disrupted global food and energy markets, prompted Finland and Sweden to join NATO, and led the International Criminal Court to issue an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin in 2023 over the deportation of Ukrainian children. Fighting was still continuing in mid-2025.

title: World population reaches 8 billion
summary: The United Nations estimated that the human population passed 8 billion, only about 11 years after it reached 7 billion.
description: The date was a symbolic UN projection rather than a precise count, since global population estimates are uncertain by a year or more. The world's population had quadrupled since the late 1920s, driven mainly by falling death rates, but growth has slowed as birth rates have dropped, and by 2022 about two-thirds of people lived in countries where fertility was below the replacement level of about 2.1 children per woman. In April 2023 India overtook China as the most populous country, according to UN estimates. UN projections suggest that world population will peak at around 10.3 billion in the 2080s, with most remaining growth in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: ChatGPT launches the generative-AI boom
summary: OpenAI released ChatGPT, a chatbot built on a large language model, which gained an estimated 100 million users within about two months.
description: ChatGPT was built on OpenAI's GPT-3.5 large language models, which use the transformer architecture introduced by Google researchers in 2017, are trained on vast amounts of text and are refined with human feedback, allowing it to write essays, code and conversation on almost any subject. Its success set off an intense race among technology companies in the United States and China, and hundreds of billions of dollars of investment in AI chips and data centres that made the chipmaker Nvidia one of the world's most valuable companies. Image generators such as DALL·E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion spread in the same period. Generative AI raised hopes for productivity and scientific progress alongside concerns about misinformation, copyright, jobs, energy use and long-term safety, prompting new rules such as the European Union's AI Act of 2024.

title: Turkey–Syria earthquakes
summary: Two powerful earthquakes, of magnitude 7.8 and 7.5, struck southern Turkey and northern Syria hours apart, killing more than 59,000 people.
description: The first shock struck before dawn on the East Anatolian Fault near Pazarcık in Kahramanmaraş province, and a second, nearly as strong, hit about nine hours later near Elbistan, together rupturing some 500 km of faults. Tens of thousands of buildings collapsed in cities such as Antakya, Kahramanmaraş and Adıyaman, and in Syria's war-torn northwest, where aid was hampered by the conflict. It was the deadliest earthquake in Turkey's modern history, with more than 53,000 deaths in Turkey and about 6,000 in Syria. Poor enforcement of building codes was widely blamed for the scale of the collapses, and hundreds of contractors and officials faced investigation.

title: Civil war erupts in Sudan
summary: Fighting broke out between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, creating the world's largest displacement and hunger crisis.
description: The Sudanese Armed Forces under Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the Rapid Support Forces under Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, had seized power together in a 2021 coup but fell out over plans to merge the RSF into the army, and fighting erupted in Khartoum on 15 April 2023. The war spread to Darfur, where the RSF was accused of ethnic massacres of the Masalit people around El Geneina, and in January 2025 the United States declared that the RSF had committed genocide. More than 12 million people had been displaced by 2025, the largest displacement crisis in the world, and famine was confirmed in parts of Darfur in 2024. Estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to around 150,000. The army retook Khartoum in March 2025, but the war continued.

title: Record global heat in 2023 and 2024
summary: 2023 and then 2024 became the hottest years on record, with 2024 the first calendar year about 1.5 °C warmer than pre-industrial times.
description: Driven mainly by human greenhouse-gas emissions, with an added boost from an El Niño that began in mid-2023, global temperatures broke monthly records from June 2023 well into 2024. The World Meteorological Organization put 2024's average at about 1.55 °C above the 1850–1900 level, although the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C limit refers to a multi-decade average rather than a single year. The period brought record ocean surface temperatures, a global coral-bleaching event, Canada's worst wildfire season on record, and deadly heatwaves from Mexico and India to the Hajj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia. Scientists continue to debate how much other factors, such as cleaner shipping fuel that reduced reflective sulphur pollution and lower cloud cover, added to the size of the jump. The marker is placed at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts in Reading, England, whose Copernicus service tracks global temperatures.

title: Chandrayaan-3 lands near the Moon's south pole
summary: India's Chandrayaan-3 made the first soft landing in the Moon's south polar region, making India the fourth nation to land on the Moon.
description: Launched from Sriharikota on 14 July 2023, the mission's Vikram lander touched down at about 69°S on the lunar near side, four years after its predecessor Chandrayaan-2 crashed during its landing attempt. The small Pragyan rover then confirmed sulphur in the surface soil and measured temperatures before both went into hibernation as the lunar night fell. The landing, days after Russia's Luna 25 crashed in the same region, was achieved on a budget of about US$75 million and was a landmark for India's space programme, run from its headquarters in Bengaluru. The Moon's polar regions are of special interest because permanently shadowed craters there may hold water ice.

title: Hamas attack on Israel and the Gaza war
summary: Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking some 250 hostages; Israel responded with a devastating war in Gaza.
description: The surprise assault from the Gaza Strip on 7 October 2023 was the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Israel declared war and launched an air and ground campaign to destroy Hamas and recover the hostages, which reduced much of Gaza to ruins, displaced most of its 2.1 million people and caused a severe humanitarian and hunger crisis. By early 2025 Gaza's health ministry reported more than 50,000 Palestinians killed, a large share of them women and children. The war spread to fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon, direct exchanges of strikes between Israel and Iran and attacks on Red Sea shipping by Yemen's Houthis, and South Africa brought a genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice. Hostages were freed in exchanges during truces in November 2023 and early 2025, and under a US-brokered ceasefire that took effect on 10 October 2025 the last living hostages were released, although a lasting settlement remained unresolved.

title: Trump wins a second, non-consecutive term
summary: Donald Trump defeated Vice-President Kamala Harris to return to the White House, the first president since Grover Cleveland to win non-consecutive terms.
description: Trump carried all seven closely contested swing states and, unlike in 2016, won the national popular vote, after a campaign dominated by inflation and immigration, while Republicans also won both houses of Congress. Harris had replaced President Joe Biden as the Democratic candidate in July 2024 after Biden withdrew following a poor debate performance. Trump had survived an assassination attempt at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, that July, and he became the first person convicted of a felony to be elected president, after a New York jury found him guilty of falsifying business records in May 2024. He was inaugurated on 20 January 2025 and quickly began a programme of sweeping tariffs, stepped-up immigration enforcement and cuts to the federal government.
